subject: physics
title: Measuring instruments and techniques
key_idea: Choose the instrument for the size and speed of the quantity and read it with care. Use callipers or micrometers for small lengths, light gates or timers for time, and a cathode-ray oscilloscope for changing voltages. Methods such as timing many oscillations improve accuracy.

blocks.text: Analogue instruments have a scale you read by eye. Digital instruments show a number. Each has a resolution that limits the reading.

items.meaning: Estimate a reading between two marks on a scale.
A fixed pointer or mark used as a reference for judging a position or timing a moving object.

items: Read an analogue scale by interpolating to about half of the smallest division.
Look at right angles to the scale to avoid parallax error.
Use analogue apparatus for length, temperature, pressure, force, angle and volume.
Use digital instruments, including a multimeter, for time, current, voltage, resistance and mass.
Record every reading to the resolution of the instrument and with its unit.
Time **multiple oscillations**, then divide, to reduce the effect of reaction time.
Use a **fiducial marker** at the centre of an oscillation, so you start and stop on the same point.
Use a set square to check that a rule is vertical or at right angles.
Use a plumb line to check that a stand or string is vertical.
Interpolate analogue scales and read them at right angles.
Timing many oscillations and using a fiducial marker improve accuracy.

sections.heading: Measuring small lengths and short times

blocks.text: A ruler is too coarse for small dimensions. Callipers and micrometers read much smaller lengths. Timing needs a stopwatch or light gates.

rows: lengths of a few cm to 1 m
diameters and thicknesses of a few mm to cm

items: Check for a zero error by closing the jaws with nothing between them. Subtract it from every reading.
Take several readings of a wire's diameter along its length and in different directions, then average.
On a vernier scale, read the main scale and add the vernier division that lines up with a main-scale mark.
On a micrometer, tighten with the ratchet so the same force is used every time.
A **stopwatch** has a resolution of 0.01 s, but human reaction time (about 0.2 s) is the larger error.
A **light gate** switches a timer on and off as an object cuts the beam, so there is no reaction-time error.
Use two gates to find a speed or acceleration, or one gate with a card of known width to find an average speed.
Callipers and micrometers measure small lengths; check the zero error first.
Light gates remove reaction-time error from timing.

blocks.text: An oscilloscope (CRO) displays a changing voltage against time. The screen is divided into squares called divisions.

items.meaning: The setting that gives the time represented by one horizontal division, for example 5 ms/div.
The setting that gives the voltage represented by one vertical division, for example 2 V/div.

items.text: Count the horizontal divisions for one complete cycle, then multiply by the time-base setting.
Use f = 1 ÷ T, with T in seconds.
Count the vertical divisions from the centre line to a peak, then multiply by the y-gain setting.

blocks.label: Frequency from the period
where: f is the frequency in hertz (Hz)
T is the period in seconds (s)

diagram.alt: An interactive. Change the oscilloscope settings and trace to see the period, frequency and amplitude.

items: Period = horizontal divisions × time-base; amplitude = vertical divisions × y-gain.
Frequency is 1 ÷ period, with the period in seconds.

checks.q: Describe how to measure the diameter of a thin wire accurately with a micrometer.
checks.a: Check and correct the zero error. Tighten with the ratchet. Measure at several places along the wire and in different directions, then take a mean.

checks.q: One cycle of a waveform covers 5.0 divisions on an oscilloscope with a time-base of 2.0 ms/div. Calculate the frequency.
Explain why a light gate gives a more accurate time than a hand-held stopwatch for a falling card.
checks.a: The gate switches the timer automatically as the card cuts the beam, so there is no reaction-time error; a stopwatch has a delay of about 0.2 s at start and stop.

items: Build a circuit from a circuit diagram using a DC supply, cells and components, in the right order and with the correct polarity for meters, diodes and LEDs.
Connect ammeters in series and voltmeters in parallel with the component.
Design a circuit, build it and check each part works before taking readings.
Use a signal generator with a loudspeaker, or an oscilloscope with a microphone, to generate and measure sound waves.
Generate and measure waves with a ripple tank, a vibration transducer or a microwave or radio-wave source.
Use a laser or other light source to investigate interference and diffraction. Never look into the beam.
Use a data logger with sensors, computer modelling or software to collect and process data.
Use ionising radiation and detectors safely: keep sources shielded, handle with tongs, keep distance and minimise time.
Choose the correct unit for each measurement and quote it with the reading.
Use the time-base and y-gain to determine the frequency and amplitude of a signal from its trace.
A trace with a horizontal line means the time-base is on and no signal is applied; a vertical line means the time-base is off.
Amplitude is measured from the centre line, so a peak-to-peak height is halved.
